previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of hypertension, aortic stenosis, chronic bronchitis, anemia, and recent pneumonia was admitted for evaluation of shortness of breath and abnormal EKG findings from his primary care visit. He denied chest pain but had mild anterior chest discomfort and chronic dyspnea unchanged from baseline. Cardiac enzymes were repeatedly normal, telemetry showed no arrhythmias, and chest imaging revealed no acute process, effectively ruling out myocardial infarction. His hypertension was managed with the addition of amlodipine due to persistently elevated blood pressure. Anemia and hyponatremia remained stable and were not actively treated. The patient's symptoms were attributed to resolving pneumonia and chronic lung disease. He was discharged home with medication adjustments and plans for outpatient follow-up and respiratory therapy evaluation.

Discharge Instructions:
 You were admitted because you had a painful left shoulder. Out 
of concern it was infected, orthopedics was consulted. A sample 
of the fluid found you had an infection with a bacteria. You 
were taken to the operating room to clean the infection out of 
your joint. The operation was successful and a drain was placed. 
You were started on an antibiotic for your infection in your 
joint, called Vancomycin. You will need to be on these 
antibiotics for at least four weeks. You will also follow up 
closely with your orthopedic physician and your primary care 
doctor. These appointments are already scheduled and below. We 
did not find a source of your infection, but the dentists came 
to evaluate your teeth and felt that this may have been the 
source. You will need to follow up with your dentist in the next 
month. We performed an echocardiogram of your heart and this was 
negative for any sources of bacteria on your heart valves. 
You will have weekly blood tests in rehab to evaluate your 
infection.

 During your hospitalization, you developed a new heart rhythm 
called atrial fibrillation. While you were in this rhythm, you 
heart rate became very fast. We gave you medicines to slow down 
your heart rate. We asked the cardiologists to evaluate you. 
Approximately 48 hours after this heart rhythm began, you 
converted back to a normal sinus rhythm on your own. No further 
intervention needed to be done. Since you were in this heart 
rhythm, Dr. ___ cardiologist, felt you should be on a 
medication called coumadin indefinitely. This medication will 
keep your blood thin to prevent blood clots. Many times, people 
who have atrial fibrillation can develop clots. This medication 
will help prevent this. You were started on a heparin drip in 
the hospital until the coumadin levels in your blood are 
therapeutic. A blood test will check if coumadin is therapeutic 
called an INR. You should have this level checked daily until 
your INR level is 2.0. Your goal is ___. 

 When you were admitted, you had a low sodium of 118. During 
your hospital stay, we restricted your fluid intake from 1200 mL 
to 1500 mLs, and your sodium level improved to 127. It was felt 
you were back to your baseline level. You should continue to 
stay on this fluid restriction and follow up with your doctor 
for further management of this.

INDICATION:  Rotator cuff tear, presents for pain.

FINDINGS:  There is worsening degenerative disease at the glenohumeral
articulation.  There are no fractures or alignment abnormalities.  

The acromion process is irregular and sclerotic without visualized connection
with the scapula. This is better visualized since the prior study, might be
related to either an os acromiale with degenerative changes or sequelae of old
trauma. These changes do not appear to reflect an acute injury.  Moderate DJD
is also noted at the acromioclavicular joint.  

There are no focal lytic or sclerotic osseous lesions.  Subchondral cystic
change and sclerosis of the glenoid and the humeral head is likely related to
DJD.  Imaged soft tissues are unremarkable.  These are worst than the study
from ___.
